propositions.text: The CEAA is a detailed procedure federal authorities must follow before environmentally impactful projects proceed.
propositions.quote: The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (“CEAA ” or “Act ”), is a detailed set of procedures that federal authorities must follow before projects that may adversely affect the environment are permitted to proceed.

propositions.text: The Act and regulations provide different levels of environmental assessment intensity depending on the project.
propositions.quote: The Act and its regulations provide for different levels of intensity with which environmental assessments are to be performed depending upon the nature of the project under scrutiny.

propositions.text: Assessment intensity determines the track: screening, comprehensive study, mediation or review panel.
propositions.quote: In practice, the intensity with which an environmental assessment should be conducted determines the “track” on which the assessment proceeds, whether by screening, comprehensive study, mediation or review panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the CEAA sets procedures with varying assessment intensity determining the environmental assessment track.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the environmental assessment track is determined by the project as proposed or by the federal authority's discretionary scoping decision.
propositions.quote: The issue in this appeal is whether the environmental assessment track is determined by the project as proposed by a proponent or by the discretionary scoping decision of the federal authority.

propositions.text: The Act and regulations require the assessment track be determined by the project as proposed; federal authorities generally cannot change that level.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the Act and regulations require that the environmental assessment track be determined according to the project as proposed; it is generally not open to a federal authority to change that level.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue and concludes the assessment track is determined by the project as proposed, not by federal discretion.

propositions.text: Red Chris seeks to develop a copper and gold open pit mine in northwestern BC.
propositions.quote: Red Chris Development Company Ltd. and BCMetals Corporation (“Red Chris”) seek to develop a copper and gold open pit mining and milling operation in northwestern British Columbia.

propositions.text: MiningWatch is a non-profit concerned with mining's environmental and social effects, especially on indigenous people.
propositions.quote: The appellant (MiningWatch) is a non‑profit society interested in the environmental, social, economic, health and cultural effects of mining and in particular its effects on indigenous people.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Red Chris's mining project and MiningWatch's environmental and indigenous concerns.

propositions.text: Red Chris submitted a project description to BC Environmental Assessment Office on October 27, 2003.
propositions.quote: On October 27, 2003, Red Chris submitted a project description to the BC Environmental Assessment Office (“BCEAO”).

propositions.text: BCEAO required an environmental assessment certificate before project proceeding.
propositions.quote: The BCEAO issued an order stating that the project would require an environmental assessment certificate before proceeding.

propositions.text: BC assessment proceeded smoothly with terms of reference, public and agency consultation, and open houses.
propositions.quote: The BC assessment proceeded smoothly. Red Chris prepared terms of reference covering all aspects of the project and made them available for comment by a working group (which included provincial and federal agencies, and the local First Nations groups). Red Chris also sought public comment on the project through several open house meetings.

propositions.text: BCEAO posted application online for public comment; public submitted several comments.
propositions.quote: Once Red Chris submitted its application, the BCEAO posted the application online for public comment. Members of the public submitted several comments in response to the proponent’s application.

propositions.text: On July 22, 2005, BCEAO concluded project unlikely to cause significant adverse effects.
propositions.quote: On July 22, 2005, the BCEAO released its environmental assessment, concluding that the project “is not likely to cause significant adverse environmental, heritage, social, economic, or health effects”.

propositions.text: On August 24, 2005, BC issued an assessment certificate.
propositions.quote: On August 24, 2005, the province issued an assessment certificate.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the BC environmental assessment process and certificate issuance for the project.

propositions.text: On about May 3, 2004, Red Chris triggered federal environmental assessment by submitting dam applications to DFO.
propositions.quote: On or about May 3, 2004, Red Chris triggered the federal environmental assessment process under ss. 5(1) (d) and 5(2) of the CEAA by submitting to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (“DFO”) applications for dams required to create a tailings impoundment area (an area in a small valley to be used for the permanent storage of mining effluent).

propositions.text: DFO concluded a federal environmental assessment was required.
propositions.quote: DFO concluded that a federal environmental assessment would be required.

propositions.text: On May 21, 2004, DFO posted notice of commencement stating it would conduct a comprehensive study of the project including mine and infrastructure.
propositions.quote: On or about May 21, 2004, a “Notice of Commencement of an environmental assessment” was posted on the Canadian Environmental Assessment Registry website stating that DFO, as a “responsible authority” (“RA”), would conduct a comprehensive study of the project and described the project as an OPEN PIT MINE WITH ASSOCIATED INFRASTRUCTURE INCLUDING TAILINGS IMPOUNDMENT AREA, ACCESS ROADS, WATER INTAKE, TRANSMISSION LINES AND ACCESSORY BUILDINGS (E.G. MAINTENANCE, CAMPSITE)

propositions.text: DFO stated comprehensive study required because ore production exceeded threshold in Comprehensive Study List Regulations.
propositions.quote: In a letter from DFO to other federal departments, DFO stated that a comprehensive study was required because the project’s proposed ore production was great enough that it fell within the provisions of the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638 (“CSL”), promulgated under the CEAA .

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the federal environmental assessment initiation and DFO's comprehensive study decision based on ore production.

propositions.text: On June 2, 2004, NRCan also became a responsible authority due to Explosives Act approval requirement.
propositions.quote: On June 2, 2004, Natural Resources Canada (“NRCan”) responded to this letter and announced that it was also an RA in addition to DFO because Red Chris required an approval under the Explosives Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-17 .

propositions.text: DFO and NRCan prepared to conduct a comprehensive study until December 9, 2004, when DFO scoped the project excluding mine and mill.
propositions.quote: DFO and NRCan prepared to conduct a comprehensive study until December 9, 2004, when DFO wrote a letter to the Canadian Environmental Assessment Agency advising that it had scoped the project such that it excluded the mine and the mill.

propositions.text: DFO finalized scope to tailings impoundment, water diversion, explosives storage/manufacturing only.
propositions.quote: DFO later finalized the scope of the project as only including the tailings impoundment area, the water diversion system with ancillary facilities and the explosives storage and/or manufacturing facility.

propositions.text: DFO determined comprehensive study unnecessary and assessment would proceed by screening due to narrowed scope.
propositions.quote: As a result, DFO determined that, as the mine and mill were no longer included in the project as scoped for environmental assessment, a comprehensive study was not necessary and the assessment would proceed by way of screening.

propositions.text: On December 14, 2004, the notice of commencement was retroactively amended to indicate screening instead of comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: On December 14, 2004, the online notice of commencement was retroactively amended to indicate that the project would be subject to a screening rather than a comprehensive study.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains how DFO and NRCan narrowed the project scope, changed assessment from comprehensive study to screening, and amended the notice.

propositions.text: On April 19, 2006, the federal screening report was released based on cooperative federal/provincial EA process.
propositions.quote: On or about April 19, 2006, the federal screening report was released. The report stated that it was “based on information collected through the cooperative federal/provincial EA [environmental assessment] process”.

propositions.text: Responsible authorities did not seek additional public comment, relying on BC assessment and public responses.
propositions.quote: The RAs did not seek additional public comment, relying instead on the BC environmental assessment and the public notice and responses under it.

propositions.text: The report concluded the project is not likely to cause significant adverse environmental effects.
propositions.quote: The report concluded that the project is not likely to cause significant adverse environmental effects.

propositions.text: On May 2, 2006, responsible authorities allowed the project to proceed and posted the screening report online.
propositions.quote: On May 2, 2006, the RAs made their decision to allow the project to proceed. A few days after this decision, the Screening Report was posted on the Canadian Environmental Assessment Registry website.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the federal screening report release, reliance on BC assessment, conclusion, and project approval.

propositions.text: MiningWatch filed judicial review application challenging decision to conduct screening rather than comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: On June 9, 2006, MiningWatch Canada filed an application in the Federal Court for judicial review of the decision to conduct a screening rather than a comprehensive study.

propositions.text: MiningWatch alleged breach of CEAA duty to conduct comprehensive study and consult public on assessment scope.
propositions.quote: It alleged a breach of the duty under the CEAA to conduct a comprehensive study and to consult the public on the scope of the assessment.

paragraphs.summary: MiningWatch applied for judicial review alleging breach of duty to conduct comprehensive study and public consultation.

propositions.text: Martineau J. allowed judicial review application.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. allowed the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Martineau J. found DFO was correct initially to require comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: He concluded that DFO had been correct in first determining that the project required a comprehensive study.

propositions.text: Martineau J. found s. 21 CEAA requires mandatory public consultation for comprehensive studies.
propositions.quote: He found that the language of s. 21 of the CEAA , as amended in 2003, made public consultation mandatory for comprehensive studies

propositions.text: Martineau J. found DFO and NRCan breached CEAA duty by scoping assessment to only federal jurisdiction aspects.
propositions.quote: and that DFO and NRCan had breached their duty under the CEAA by scoping the environmental assessment to include only those aspects of the project that fell under federal jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: Martineau J. allowed review, finding DFO initially correct and that public consultation was mandatory but breached by narrowing scope.

propositions.text: Martineau J. quashed DFO's permits and prohibited further action until consultation and comprehensive study completed.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. quashed the decision of DFO to issue permits and approvals to Red Chris and prohibited further action by DFO and NRCan until they had conducted public consultation under s. 21 , completed a comprehensive study and complied with all other prerequisites to permit the project to be carried out.

paragraphs.summary: Martineau J. quashed permits and prohibited further action until consultation and comprehensive study done.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal allowed appeal, set aside Martineau J.'s order, dismissed judicial review.
propositions.quote: Desjardins J.A., writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, allowed the appeal.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found 'project' means 'project as scoped' by federal RA for environmental assessment purposes.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal found that “project” for federal environmental assessment purposes means “project as scoped” by a federal RA.

propositions.text: Comprehensive study and public consultation mandatory only if project as scoped by RA is listed in CSL.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, a comprehensive study and public consultation are only mandatory where a project as scoped by the RA is listed in the CSL.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal relied on earlier decisions Sunpine and TrueNorth that 'project' means 'project as scoped'.
propositions.quote: Desjardins J.A. relied on the Federal Court of Appeal’s earlier decisions in Friends of the West Country Assn. v. Canada (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans), [2000] 2 F.C. 263 (“Sunpine”), and Prairie Acid Rain Coalition v. Canada (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans), 2006 FCA 31, [2006] 3 F.C.R. 610 (“TrueNorth”), and its conclusion that “project” in s. 5(1) (d) and s. 15(3) of the Act means “project as scoped”.

propositions.text: Despite amendment to s. 21, TrueNorth remains binding as introductory text in s. 21(1) unchanged.
propositions.quote: Despite a recent amendment to s. 21 , Desjardins J.A. found that TrueNorth was still binding because the introductory text in s. 21(1) was not altered by the amendment.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal reversed, holding 'project' means 'project as scoped' and comprehensive study depends on that scope.

propositions.text: The issue is whether DFO and NRCan have discretion under CEAA to determine assessment track as screening or comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: The issue in the present case is whether DFO and NRCan, as responsible authorities under the CEAA , have been conferred discretion under the CEAA to determine whether an environmental assessment proceeds by way of a screening or comprehensive study.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue whether DFO and NRCan have discretion to choose assessment track under CEAA.

propositions.text: Relevant legislative and regulatory provisions are attached in the Appendix.
propositions.quote: The relevant legislative and regulatory provisions are attached in the Appendix.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes relevant legislative and regulatory provisions are appended.

propositions.text: CEAA establishes a federal environmental assessment process integrating environmental considerations into planning and decision making.
propositions.quote: The CEAA is, in the words of its formal title, “[a]n Act to establish a federal environmental assessment process”. It provides a process for integrating environmental considerations into planning and decision making (CEAA , Preamble; Friends of the Oldman River Society v. Canada (Minister of Transport), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 3, at p. 71).

propositions.text: The Act sets five procedural options or tracks for environmental assessment depending on the project nature.
propositions.quote: In broad overview, the Act sets forth five potential procedural options or tracks for environmental assessment depending upon the nature of the project, i.e. the physical work or physical activity to be reviewed.

propositions.text: The five tracks vary in assessment intensity: No Assessment, Screening, Comprehensive Study, Mediation, Review Panel.
propositions.quote: These five tracks vary in levels of intensity of assessment: 1. No Assessment 2. Screening 3. Comprehensive Study 4. Mediation 5. Review Panel (1) No Assessment

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CEAA's five environmental assessment procedural tracks varying by project nature and intensity.

propositions.text: Section 7(1) excludes projects on the Exclusion List or emergencies from environmental assessment.
propositions.quote: Section 7(1) provides that if a project is described on the Exclusion List Regulations, 2007, SOR/2007‑108, or is required in response to an emergency, no environmental assessment need be carried out.

propositions.text: Projects on the Exclusion List are considered to have insignificant environmental effects.
propositions.quote: Projects on this list are considered to have insignificant environmental effects.

propositions.text: Examples include maintenance or repair of physical work outside protected areas.
propositions.quote: Projects in the Exclusion List Regulations, 2007 include, for example, the proposed maintenance or repair of a physical work (so long as it is not carried out in a national park, park reserve, national historic site or historic canal) (Sch. 1, s. 1).

paragraphs.summary: The court describes s.7(1) excluding certain projects from assessment as insignificant environmental effects.

propositions.text: Screening is the least intense assessment track for projects not on exclusion or comprehensive study lists.
propositions.quote: The least intense environmental assessment track is termed a “screening”. If a proposed project does not appear in the exclusion list or the comprehensive study list (discussed below), then a screening is required pursuant to s. 18 of the Act .

propositions.text: Screening applies to projects with some potential adverse effects but not significant enough for more intense assessments.
propositions.quote: Projects requiring a screening are those considered to have some potential for adverse environmental effects, but those effects are not considered to be significant enough to warrant the more intense assessments discussed below.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains screening applies to projects with some potential adverse effects but not significant enough for intense assessment.

propositions.text: Comprehensive studies, mediation, and review panels arise from projects listed in the Comprehensive Study List (CSL).
propositions.quote: Finally, comprehensive studies, mediation and review panels all arise from the listing of a proposed project in the CSL.

propositions.text: Under s. 21.1(1), Minister of Environment has three options for CSL projects: comprehensive study, mediation, or review panel.
propositions.quote: Under s. 21.1(1) of the Act , if a project is described in the CSL, the Minister of the Environment has three options. One is to refer the project to an RA (generally a federal department or agency) to proceed with a comprehensive study. A second is to refer the project to a mediator if all interested parties agree. A third is to refer the project to a review panel.

propositions.text: Projects in CSL are considered likely to have significant adverse environmental effects.
propositions.quote: Projects in the CSL are those considered likely to have significant adverse environmental effects (CSL, Preamble).

propositions.text: A mine or mill above specified capacity is listed in the CSL.
propositions.quote: A mine or mill with a proposed capacity above the specified threshold is listed in the CSL (CSL, Sch., s. 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CSL projects likely have significant effects and Minister chooses assessment method among three options.

propositions.text: CSL projects have mandatory public consultation at outset and throughout assessment (ss. 21-23).
propositions.quote: Some of the more important requirements pertaining to projects in the CSL that do not apply to projects that require only a screening assessment are: (1) Mandatory public consultation at the outset and throughout the environmental assessment process (ss. 21 -23 ).

propositions.text: CSL projects have government funding to facilitate public participation (s. 58(1.1)).
propositions.quote: (2) A government funding program to facilitate public participation in the environmental assessment process (s. 58(1.1)).

propositions.text: Minister determines whether assessment is comprehensive study, mediation, or review panel (s. 21.1).
propositions.quote: (3) Determination by the Minister as to whether the environmental assessment should be conducted as a comprehensive study by the RA or be referred to mediation or to a review panel (s. 21.1).

propositions.text: Minister determines if project will cause significant adverse environmental effects (s. 23).
propositions.quote: (4) Determination by the Minister rather than an RA as to whether the project will cause significant adverse effects to the environment (s. 23).

propositions.text: CSL projects require assessment of project purpose, alternatives, environmental effects of alternatives (s. 16(2)).
propositions.quote: (5) Assessment of the purpose of the project and consideration of alternative means of carrying out the project and the environmental effects of the alternatives (s. 16(2)).

propositions.text: CSL projects require follow-up program (s. 16(2)).
propositions.quote: (6) The need for a follow-up program (s. 16(2)).

propositions.text: CSL projects require capacity of affected renewable resources to meet present and future needs (s. 16(2)).
propositions.quote: (7) The capacity of affected renewable resources to meet present and future needs (s. 16(2)).

propositions.text: CSL projects have more intensive assessment, ministerial oversight, and mandatory public consultation than screening.
propositions.quote: Generally speaking, in comparison to a screening, projects in the CSL are subjected to more intensive assessment, ministerial oversight and mandatory public consultation.

paragraphs.summary: The court lists CSL project requirements including public consultation, funding, ministerial decisions, and more intensive assessment.

propositions.text: Section 21 initiates procedures RAs must follow when project is listed in CSL.
propositions.quote: The provision under scrutiny in the present appeal is s. 21 of the CEAA . Section 21 initiates the set of procedures that RAs must follow when a project is listed in the CSL.

propositions.text: Section 21(1) requires RAs to ensure public consultation on proposed project scope, assessment factors, and ability of study to address issues.
propositions.quote: 21. (1) Where a project is described in the comprehensive study list, the responsible authority shall ensure public consultation with respect to the proposed scope of the project for the purposes of the environmental assessment, the factors proposed to be considered in its assessment, the proposed scope of those factors and the ability of the comprehensive study to address issues relating to the project.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.21 requires RAs to ensure public consultation on project scope and assessment factors for CSL projects.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal and government argue s.15(1) discretion to scope project includes discretion to determine assessment track.
propositions.quote: The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal and the positions of the government and Red Chris on the proper interpretation of s. 21 are largely based on their interpretation of the application of s. 15(1) of the CEAA . They argue that s. 15(1) , which grants the discretion to “scope” the project (i.e. define what aspects of the project will be included in the federal environmental assessment), includes the discretion to “track” the project (i.e. determine the level of assessment).

propositions.text: They argue determining assessment track and project scope are the same step in the assessment process.
propositions.quote: In other words, they argue that determining the assessment track and determining the scope of the project are the same step in the assessment process.

propositions.text: Section 15(1) provides that project scope is determined by RA or Minister after consultation.
propositions.quote: The “scoping” provision, s. 15(1) , provides: 15. (1) The scope of the project in relation to which an environmental assessment is to be conducted shall be determined by (a) the responsible authority; or (b) where the project is referred to a mediator or a review panel, the Minister, after consulting with the responsible authority.

paragraphs.summary: The respondents argue s.15(1) discretion to scope project includes discretion to determine assessment track, equating scoping and tracking.

propositions.text: s. 15(1) is general and lets RA determine project scope for environmental assessment, possibly narrower than proponent's proposal
propositions.quote: s. 15(1) is of “general application” and confers on an RA the discretion to determine the scope of the project in relation to which an environmental assessment is to be conducted

propositions.text: RA can scope project narrower than CSL listing, requiring only screening not comprehensive study
propositions.quote: the project as scoped by the RA is not in the CSL and therefore requires only a screening and not a comprehensive study

propositions.text: Support DFO and NRCan approach scoping project as tailings impoundment, water diversion, explosives storage, none in CSL
propositions.quote: They, therefore, support the approach taken in this case by DFO and NRCan which scoped the project as the tailings impoundment area, water diversion system and explosives storage/manufacturing facility, none of which are listed in the CSL

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue s. 15(1) lets RA scope project narrower than proponent's proposal, requiring only screening, supporting DFO and NRCan's approach.

propositions.text: ss. 18-20 (screening) and 21-24 (comprehensive study) follow s. 15, so 'project' in ss. 18 and 21 is subject to s. 15(1) scoping discretion
propositions.quote: Red Chris and the government argue that these “screening” and “comprehensive study” provisions follow directly after the “general” provisions which include s. 15(1) . Therefore, the reference to “project” in ss. 18 and 21 is subject to the scoping discretion in s. 15(1)

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue ss. 18 and 21's 'project' is subject to s. 15(1) scoping discretion because these provisions follow s. 15.

propositions.text: Interpretation gives RAs flexibility to address project specifics, jurisdiction, expertise, provincial coordination, and avoid duplication
propositions.quote: Red Chris and the government also argue that their interpretation provides the RAs with the flexibility required to address the specific circumstances of each project

propositions.text: Appellant's interpretation leads to rigid, inflexible, arbitrary environmental assessment approach
propositions.quote: They argue that the appellant’s interpretation, which provides that “project” means “project as proposed by the proponent”, leads to a rigid, inflexible and arbitrary approach to environmental assessment

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue their interpretation gives RAs flexibility and appellant's leads to rigid, arbitrary assessments.

propositions.text: Rationale exists to limit duplication by scoping federal assessment narrower than proponent's project focusing on federal jurisdiction and approvals
propositions.quote: Where projects are subject to environmental assessment by both provincial and federal authorities, it is not unreasonable to think that such projects should not be subject to two, duplicative, environmental assessments

paragraphs.summary: Court finds rationale to limit duplication by scoping federal assessment narrower than proponent's project.

propositions.text: s. 12(4) CEAA allows federal RA to cooperate with provinces for environmental assessment
propositions.quote: s. 12(4) of the CEAA provides that in such cases, a federal RA may cooperate with the province in respect of the environmental assessment

propositions.text: Regulations and agreements exist for federal-provincial coordination and harmonization of environmental assessments
propositions.quote: Detailed provisions for coordination are set out in the Regulations Respecting the Coordination by Federal Authorities of Environmental Assessment Procedures and Requirements, SOR/97-181, the Canada‑British Columbia Agreement for Environmental Assessment Cooperation (2004), and similar provincial-federal harmonization agreements

propositions.text: Respondents' policy arguments on duplication and coordination are recognized in CEAA and regulations
propositions.quote: Red Chris and the government’s policy arguments regarding duplication and coordination have been recognized in the CEAA and its regulations

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CEAA and regulations provide for federal-provincial cooperation, recognizing respondents' duplication and coordination arguments.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal decisions TrueNorth and Sunpine relied on by respondents and FCA cannot be sustained here
propositions.quote: I am of the opinion that the approach of the Federal Court of Appeal and that advocated by Red Chris and the government cannot be sustained

propositions.text: These reasons govern over inconsistent prior decisions relied on by respondents and FCA
propositions.quote: To the extent that the decisions relied on by Red Chris, the government and the Federal Court of Appeal are inconsistent with the analysis that follows, these reasons now govern

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects prior FCA decisions relied on by respondents and FCA, stating these reasons now govern.

propositions.text: Court must interpret Act based on text and context
propositions.quote: The duty of this Court is to interpret the Act based on its text and context

propositions.text: RA does not have discretion to conduct only screening when proposed project is listed in CSL
propositions.quote: it is not within the discretion of the RA to conduct only a screening when a proposed project is listed in the CSL

paragraphs.summary: Court states it must interpret Act by text and context and finds RA cannot limit assessment to screening if project is in CSL.

propositions.text: Definition of 'project' in s. 2 CEAA means 'project as proposed by proponent'
propositions.quote: The English definition of “project” expressly uses the word “proposed” and therefore means “project as proposed by the proponent”

propositions.text: French 'projet' implicitly includes proposal notion, supporting restricted meaning
propositions.quote: implicit in the French meaning of the word “projet” is the notion of proposal

propositions.text: Common meaning favors restricted meaning if French broader (Schreiber v. Canada)
propositions.quote: the common meaning would favour the more restricted meaning (see Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 269, at para. 56, per LeBel J.)

propositions.text: Starting point is statutory definition of project as 'project as proposed'
propositions.quote: Therefore, the starting point of this analysis is that the statutory definition of project is “project as proposed”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds statutory definition of 'project' means 'project as proposed' supported by English and French definitions and precedent.

propositions.text: Defined term 'project' applies unless displaced by express words or necessary implication
propositions.quote: displacement of the defined term requires express words or necessarily implied context that Parliament did not intend for the definition to apply

propositions.text: Nothing in ss. 18 or 21 suggests 'project' definition is displaced by RA scoping under s. 15
propositions.quote: There is nothing in s. 18 or 21 to suggest that the term “project” as defined is not applicable or is displaced by the project as scoped by the RA under s. 15

paragraphs.summary: Court finds defined term 'project' applies in ss. 18 and 21; no displacement by RA scoping under s. 15.

propositions.text: CSL English version describes projects as proposals, supporting 'project as proposed' interpretation
propositions.quote: The English version of the CSL describes projects in terms of proposals

propositions.text: French CSL version uses 'projet' which implies proposal, not 'project as scoped'
propositions.quote: implicit in the French definition of “projet” is the notion of proposal... there is certainly nothing in the term “projet” that suggests it means “project as scoped”

propositions.text: Opening words of s. 21 should be interpreted as 'project as proposed' not 'project as scoped'
propositions.quote: the opening words of s. 21 should be interpreted as “[w]here a project [as proposed] is described in the comprehensive study list” and not “[w]here a project [as scoped by the RA] is described in the comprehensive study list”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CSL language supports interpreting s. 21 'project' as 'project as proposed', not 'project as scoped'.

propositions.text: Regulations language consistent with Act's interpretation of 'project as proposed'
propositions.quote: the language in the regulations in the present case is consistent with the interpretation gleaned from the Act itself

propositions.text: Regulations completing statutory scheme are mutually informing and can be considered in interpretation
propositions.quote: When regulations are made to complete the statutory scheme, they are clearly intended to operate together and to be mutually informing

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting considering regulations in statutory interpretation (R. v. Campbell, Monsanto)
propositions.quote: See also Binnie J. in R. v. Campbell... and Deschamps J. in Monsanto Canada Inc. v. Ontario...

paragraphs.summary: Court finds regulations consistent with Act and may be considered in interpreting 'project' definition.

propositions.text: Minister has authority under s. 58(1)(i) to prescribe projects requiring comprehensive study
propositions.quote: The CEAA grants the Minister the authority to prescribe that certain projects or classes of projects are subject to a comprehensive study

propositions.text: Respondents' interpretation would subordinate Minister's authority to RA's discretion under s. 15(1)
propositions.quote: Red Chris and the government’s interpretation of s. 21 would render this authority subject to the overriding authority of the RA

propositions.text: Presumption is Minister's decisions override RA's, not vice versa
propositions.quote: The presumption in Canada... must be the other way around

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister's authority to prescribe comprehensive studies should override RA's discretion, contrary to respondents' view.

propositions.text: Disagrees with FCA that context supports RA scoping interpretation
propositions.quote: I am unable to agree with the Federal Court of Appeal’s finding that there is “nothing in the context of the CEAA which indicates . . . a different interpretation from [the project as scoped by the RA]”

propositions.text: CSL includes projects Minister determined likely to have significant adverse effects
propositions.quote: The CSL includes classes of projects which the Minister has determined are likely to have significant adverse environmental effects

propositions.text: Parliament intended Minister to determine which projects require comprehensive study, not RA
propositions.quote: Parliament intended the Minister to determine which projects did or did not require comprehensive study, not the RA

propositions.text: Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement supports Minister's role in determining projects requiring comprehensive study
propositions.quote: The Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement... supports that view

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees with FCA, finds Minister determines projects requiring comprehensive study, supported by regulatory statement.

propositions.text: Correct interpretation of 'project' in ss. 18 and 21 is 'project as proposed', not 'project as scoped'
propositions.quote: the correct interpretation is “project as proposed” and not “project as scoped”

propositions.text: Determination of comprehensive study requirement is not RA's discretion; mandatory if project as proposed is in CSL
propositions.quote: If the project as proposed is listed in the CSL, a comprehensive study is mandatory

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes 'project' means 'project as proposed' and comprehensive study is mandatory if project is in CSL.

propositions.text: How does s. 15(1) discretion to scope project fit within CEAA scheme?
propositions.quote: How, then, does the discretion conferred on the RA or Minister under s. 15(1) to determine the scope of a project for the environmental assessment fit within the scheme of the Act ?

propositions.text: Tracking and scoping are distinct; RA generally cannot determine assessment track but can determine scope once track set
propositions.quote: tracking and scoping are distinct steps in the CEAA process. Generally, the RA does not have the discretion to determine the assessment track. However... the RA does have the discretion to determine the scope

paragraphs.summary: Court poses question on s. 15(1) discretion and finds tracking and scoping distinct; RA can scope after track set.

propositions.text: For projects not in CSL, screening is conducted per RA's scope decision under s. 15(1)(a), subject to ss. 15(2) and (3)
propositions.quote: In the case of a project not in the CSL, a screening is conducted in accordance with the scope of the project as determined by the RA under s. 15(1) (a), subject to the requirements of s. 15(2) and (3)

propositions.text: RA's scoping decision is determinative for screening projects
propositions.quote: The RA’s scoping decision is determinative

paragraphs.summary: Court finds for projects not in CSL, RA's scoping decision governs screening, subject to ss. 15(2) and (3).

propositions.text: For projects in CSL, RA determines scope for comprehensive study after public consultation under s. 21(1)
propositions.quote: The RA... determines the proposed scope of the project for purposes of the comprehensive study

propositions.text: RA reports scope and public consultation results to Minister under s. 21(2)(a) and recommends continuing comprehensive study or referral
propositions.quote: Under s. 21(2)(a), the RA reports to the Minister on its determination of the scope... and recommends to the Minister to continue with the environmental assessment by means of a comprehensive study... or that the Minister refer the project to a mediation or review panel

paragraphs.summary: Court finds for CSL projects, RA scopes project, consults public, reports to Minister, and recommends study or referral.

propositions.text: Minister may remit project to RA for comprehensive study or refer to mediator/review panel under s. 21.1(1)
propositions.quote: The Minister may remit the project to the RA to conduct the comprehensive study... or refer the project to a mediator or to a review panel

propositions.text: If referred to mediator/review panel, Minister determines scope after consulting RA under s. 15(1)(b)
propositions.quote: the scope of the project is determined by the Minister after consulting with the RA pursuant to s. 15(1) (b)

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Minister may remit study to RA or refer to panel; if panel, Minister determines scope after RA consultation.

propositions.text: s. 15(1) grants discretion to RA or Minister to scope project; limited by s. 15(3) requiring assessment of all undertakings
propositions.quote: Section 15(1) grants the discretion to scope to either the Minister... or the RA. However, the exercise of this discretion is limited by s. 15(3)

propositions.text: Minimum scope is project as proposed; RA or Minister may enlarge scope under ss. 15(2) or (3)
propositions.quote: the minimum scope is the project as proposed by the proponent, and the RA or Minister has the discretion to enlarge the scope

propositions.text: s. 15(2) allows combining related projects into single project for assessment
propositions.quote: The RA or Minister is also granted further discretion by s. 15(2) to combine related proposed projects into a single project for the purposes of assessment

paragraphs.summary: Court explains s. 15 grants scoping discretion limited by s. 15(3); minimum scope is proposed project; scope may be enlarged or combined.

propositions.text: Scoping discretion under ss. 15(2) and (3) is exception to general rule that assessment level is based on project as proposed
propositions.quote: the scoping discretion under s. 15(2) and (3) acts as an exception to the general proposition that the level of assessment is determined solely based on the project as proposed by the proponent

propositions.text: Proponent could engage in 'project splitting' to avoid assessment obligations
propositions.quote: a proponent could engage in “project splitting” by representing part of a project as the whole, or proposing several parts of a project as independent projects in order to circumvent additional assessment obligations

propositions.text: If RA or Minister enlarges scope combining projects, project may move from screening to comprehensive study
propositions.quote: Where the RA or Minister considers all matters in relation to the project as proposed, the resulting scope places the project in the CSL. Where this occurs, the project would be subject to a comprehensive study

paragraphs.summary: Court finds scoping discretion is exception to rule; project splitting risk exists; enlarged scope may trigger comprehensive study.

propositions.text: For federal environmental assessment, a project includes the entire project as proposed by the proponent.
propositions.quote: while, for federal environmental assessment purposes, a project will include the entire project as proposed

propositions.text: Responsible Authorities (RAs) can minimize duplication using coordination mechanisms in the Act.
propositions.quote: the RAs can, and should, minimize duplication by using the coordination mechanisms provided for in the Act

propositions.text: Federal and provincial governments can adopt mutually agreeable terms for coordinating environmental assessments under s. 58(1)(c) and (d).
propositions.quote: federal and provincial governments can adopt mutually agreeable terms for coordinating environmental assessments (s. 58(1) (c) and (d))

propositions.text: Full use of coordination authority reduces unnecessary, costly, inefficient duplication.
propositions.quote: Full use of this authority would serve to reduce unnecessary, costly and inefficient duplication

propositions.text: Cooperation and coordination are procedures expressed in the CEAA (see s. 12(4)).
propositions.quote: Cooperation and coordination are the procedures expressed in the CEAA (see s. 12(4) )

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that a project includes the entire proposed project, RAs should minimize duplication using coordination mechanisms in the Act, and cooperation is expressed in CEAA.

propositions.text: The federal environmental assessment should have been conducted for the project as proposed by Red Chris, described in the CSL.
propositions.quote: the federal environmental assessment should have been conducted for the project as proposed by Red Chris. The proposed project was described in the CSL

propositions.text: Section 21 requirements applied to the project as proposed by Red Chris.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the requirements of s. 21 applied

propositions.text: RAs could use federal-provincial coordination tools but still had to comply with CEAA provisions for comprehensive studies.
propositions.quote: The RAs were free to use any and all federal-provincial coordination tools available, but they were still required to comply with the provisions of the CEAA pertaining to comprehensive studies

propositions.text: RAs acted without statutory authority by conducting a screening instead of a comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: The RAs in this case acted without statutory authority by conducting a screening

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the federal assessment should have been comprehensive for Red Chris's proposed project, but RAs unlawfully conducted a screening.

propositions.text: The trial judge's remedy was under s. 18.1(3) of the Federal Courts Act, which allows orders or declarations on judicial review.
propositions.quote: The remedy awarded by the trial judge was pursuant to the discretion conferred upon him under s. 18.1(3) of the Federal Courts Act

propositions.text: Section 18.1(3) allows the Federal Court to order acts or declare decisions invalid on judicial review.
propositions.quote: (3) On an application for judicial review, the Federal Court may (a) order a federal board... or (b) declare invalid or unlawful...

propositions.text: Whether this Court may and should intervene with respect to remedy is the question here.
propositions.quote: The question here is whether this Court may and should intervene with respect to remedy

propositions.text: The test for appellate review of judicial discretion is whether the first instance judge considered all relevant factors.
propositions.quote: The test for appellate review of the exercise of judicial discretion is whether the judge at first instance has given weight to all relevant considerations

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the trial judge's remedy under s. 18.1(3) and the appellate test for reviewing judicial discretion on remedy.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not consider several relevant and significant factors when granting broad relief.
propositions.quote: the learned trial judge did not take account of a number of relevant and significant considerations

propositions.text: Because of this omission, the trial judge granted broader relief than appropriate.
propositions.quote: Because of this, he granted broader relief than was appropriate

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge granted overly broad relief by not considering relevant factors.

propositions.text: Trial judge set aside RAs' screening decision and prohibited permits until a comprehensive study and decision under s. 37.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. set aside the RAs’ decision to proceed by way of screening and prohibited the issuing of permits... until the completion of a comprehensive study pursuant to s. 21 and... a decision... pursuant to s. 37

propositions.text: The parties were ordered to substantially redo the environmental assessment, which the court finds unwarranted.
propositions.quote: the parties have been ordered to substantially redo the environmental assessment. I do not think such relief is warranted

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the trial judge ordered a redo of the environmental assessment but finds such relief unwarranted.

propositions.text: Trial judge expressed suspicion of RAs' motives in downgrading assessment to screening after project was included in CSL.
propositions.quote: his reasons indicate a suspicion of the motive of the RAs

propositions.text: Environmental assessment was converted to screening on Dec 9, 2004 due to new information and TrueNorth decision.
propositions.quote: environmental assessment was converted to a screening assessment on or about December 9, 2004, because of new information and because of the issuance of the TrueNorth decision

propositions.text: Trial judge quoted DFO letter explaining RAs were influenced by new info and TrueNorth decision.
propositions.quote: the trial judge, in his reasons, quoted a letter of DFO dated December 9, 2004... explaining that the RAs were influenced by new information and by the TrueNorth decision

propositions.text: It is difficult to fault RAs for following a Federal Court decision on the matter.
propositions.quote: It is difficult to fault the RAs for following a decision of the Federal Court on the very matter with which they were dealing

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the trial judge's suspicion of RAs' motives but finds RAs acted reasonably following new info and a Federal Court decision.

propositions.text: Red Chris will be prejudiced by delay and costs from the trial judge's order, but Red Chris did nothing wrong.
propositions.quote: although it is Red Chris that will be prejudiced by incurring further delay and costs... Red Chris did nothing wrong

propositions.text: The environmental assessment approach was determined by the government, not Red Chris.
propositions.quote: The approach to the environmental assessment was determined by the government

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Red Chris will suffer delay and costs but was not at fault; the government determined the assessment approach.

propositions.text: Red Chris cooperated fully with BCEAO environmental assessment, proposed terms of reference including agencies and First Nations.
propositions.quote: Red Chris cooperated fully with the environmental assessment conducted by the BCEAO. It proposed terms of reference for a working group which included federal and provincial agencies and local First Nation groups

propositions.text: Red Chris sought public comment via open house meetings; BCEAO posted application online for public comment.
propositions.quote: Red Chris sought public comment on the project through several open house meetings... BCEAO posted the application online for public comment

propositions.text: Public submitted several comments in response to Red Chris application.
propositions.quote: members of the public submitted several comments in response to the Red Chris application

propositions.text: These facts were not considered by the trial judge in granting relief.
propositions.quote: These facts do not appear to have been considered by the trial judge in exercising his discretion to grant relief

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Red Chris cooperated fully with the assessment and public consultation, but the trial judge did not consider these facts.

propositions.text: MiningWatch stated in a letter it brought this application as a test case of federal obligations under s. 21.
propositions.quote: MiningWatch stated that it “brought this application as a test case of the federal government’s obligations under section 21”

propositions.text: Parties in test cases may still want to preserve claims, but this is not such a case.
propositions.quote: It would be incorrect to say that the parties in test cases may not still be interested in preserving their claims... However, this is not such a case

paragraphs.summary: The court notes MiningWatch brought this as a test case and finds this case is not about preserving claims.

propositions.text: MiningWatch has no proprietary or pecuniary interest in the outcome.
propositions.quote: MiningWatch says it has no proprietary or pecuniary interest in the outcome of the proceedings

propositions.text: MiningWatch did not participate in BCEAO environmental assessment; first involvement was judicial review.
propositions.quote: MiningWatch did not participate in the environmental assessment conducted by the BCEAO. Its first involvement was in commencing judicial review

propositions.text: MiningWatch brought no evidence of dissatisfaction with BCEAO or RAs assessments or process.
propositions.quote: It has not brought forward any evidence of dissatisfaction with the environmental assessments conducted by the BCEAO or the RAs; nor is there evidence of dissatisfaction with the assessment process from anyone else

propositions.text: MiningWatch brought judicial review as a test case of federal obligations under s. 21 and did not challenge substantive scoping decision.
propositions.quote: MiningWatch says it has brought this judicial review as a test case of the federal government’s obligations under s. 21 . Indeed, they made a strategic decision not to challenge the substantive scoping decision

propositions.text: This is an appropriate case to accept MiningWatch's position at face value and grant a declaration on s. 21 obligations.
propositions.quote: This is an appropriate case in which to take the position expressed by MiningWatch at face value. A declaration as to the proper interpretation of s. 21 and the obligations of the federal government achieves MiningWatch’s stated objective

paragraphs.summary: MiningWatch argues it has no pecuniary interest and brought this as a test case; the court accepts this and grants a declaration on s. 21.

propositions.text: The appropriate relief is to allow judicial review and declare RAs erred in failing to conduct a comprehensive study.
propositions.quote: the appropriate relief in this case would be to allow the application for judicial review and declare that the RAs erred in failing to conduct a comprehensive study

propositions.text: The court would decline to grant any further relief under s. 18.1(3) of the Federal Courts Act.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to s. 18.1(3) of the Federal Courts Act , I would decline to grant any further relief

paragraphs.summary: The court would allow judicial review, declare RAs erred, but decline further relief under the Federal Courts Act.

propositions.text: Exercising discretion to grant declaratory relief without redoing assessment allows a non-compliant process to stand.
propositions.quote: the result is to allow a process found not to comply with the requirements of the CEAA to stand in this case

propositions.text: The court has discretion to deny or limit remedies even if appellant is entitled to them, but must exercise with great care.
propositions.quote: the court has the power to exercise its discretion not to grant such a remedy... it must be exercised with the greatest care

propositions.text: Discretionary power to deny remedies must be exercised carefully to avoid undermining rule of law (Wade and Forsyth, Immeubles Port Louis).
propositions.quote: because such discretionary power may make inroads upon the rule of law, it must be exercised with the greatest care. See Sir William Wade and C. Forsyth... and Immeubles Port Louis Ltée v. Lafontaine

propositions.text: Balance of convenience considerations apply in discretionary relief decisions (Brown and Evans, Khosa).
propositions.quote: balance of convenience considerations are involved. See D. J. M. Brown and J. M. Evans... referred to by Binnie J. in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa

propositions.text: Balance of convenience includes disproportionate impact on parties or third parties.
propositions.quote: Such considerations will include any disproportionate impact on the parties or the interests of third parties

propositions.text: MiningWatch's interest is legal declaration; no justification to require Red Chris to repeat assessment when substantive decisions not challenged.
propositions.quote: The focus of MiningWatch’s interest as a public interest litigant is the legal point... I can see no justification in requiring Red Chris to repeat the environmental assessment process when there was no challenge to the substantive decisions made by the RAs

paragraphs.summary: The court explains discretion to limit remedies, balancing convenience and impact, and finds no justification to require Red Chris to redo assessment.

propositions.text: The court would allow the appeal with costs on a party-party basis, allow judicial review, and declare RAs erred in assessment scope.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal with costs throughout on a party and party basis, allow the application for judicial review and issue a declaration that the RAs erred

propositions.text: The court declines to grant any further relief beyond the declaration.
propositions.quote: I would decline to grant any further relief

propositions.text: Solicitor-client costs are not awarded as there is no misconduct or other reason.
propositions.quote: Although requested by MiningWatch, this is not a case for solicitor-client costs. There is no misconduct or other reason for an award other than the usual party-party award of costs

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal with party-party costs, grants judicial review and declaration, but declines further relief or solicitor-client costs.
